You're right that frequencies at exactly half the sample rate will not be reproduced at all (and frequencies close to half the sample rate will be attenuated), you can see these notches in the frequency spectrum if you apply sample rate reduction to noise or a harmonically rich sound. But the frequency isn't limited to half the sample rate. You will still get audio information if you try to record a frequency higher than half the sample rate, it will just end up being the wrong frequency. Hence, aliasing. The frequency you hear will be represented by 2N-F where N is half the sample rate and F is the recorded frequency.

There may not be benchmarks out there persay for audio workstations/DAWS, but the specs are out there to make a determination. And those 3 industries can cover all the baselines you need to figure out what goes in your rig. Gaming is going to be GPU heavy, so hardly any relevance in your decision for building a rig. Video production is mixed with GPU rendering as well as single core and multi-core processes. And photoshop is primarily CPU bound, but not entirely. At the end of the day, your DAW needs fast, single core, low latency processing. Increased core count can distribute some loads within the daw, but the bottleneck will always be your clock rate and single core processing power. I just upgraded my PC this weekend, granted some specs are overkill, but i bought the parts from a friend for cheap so I can’t complain. I got a Ryzen 8 Core/16 thread unlocked, clocked at 4.6 GhZ, Strix X570-E, 2080TI, 32 GB 3200 MhZ Dominator Platinum Ram, and a 1TB SSD connected via SATA. My old rig was an X99 Gigabyte G1 Gaming motherboard, 4 core xeon, 32 GB Dominator Ram, and an HDD. Before upgrading Ableton hovered nominally at 7-9% CPU load just with an empty project, could hardly run Serum 2, and would crash constantly when doing huge voiced saws/sounds. So much so I was constantly producing under 44.1K sample rate, and had to use a ridiculously high buffer size. So i had tons of round trip latency in my system, but was the only way I could make due with my Pc at the time. I stress tested my new Ryzen this weekend, and it took 3 OSC in Serum 2, with 16 voices each, playing 10 keys simultaneously (480 voices) for my session to shit out. My CPU utilization is at 0% nominally now, and i’ve yet to open a normal session/project and see utilization over 30% at peak processing times. So there aren’t many benchmarks out there to determine pure functionality within a DAW/Audio Workstation, but the specs, knowledge, and resources are out there to make an informed decision as to what you should and should not put in your rig.

If the effective sample rate is boosted, nearly all of the digital artefacts are produced above 20kHz and can then be filtered out when down sampled back to the project rate. The more non-linearity (distortion) in the processing, the more important handling the artefacts becomes. So you really want it done well on guitar amp sims, but it's probably irrelevant for a clean reverb plugin for example.

Whenever you perform any processing on your sound that involves resampling (tuning, stretching, reverb, delay..) you will introduce sampling artifacts. The higher your source sample rate the fewer those artifacts. Always work with the highest sample rate possible when producing and only downsample during export for best results.
